nameStory: The Atlantic white-sided dolphin gets its name from the distinctive white patches that streak along both sides of its sleek body, creating bold racing stripes against its darker coloration. This eye-catching pattern makes it one of the most easily recognizable dolphins in the North Atlantic Ocean. The name perfectly captures both its Atlantic Ocean home and its most striking visual feature.
description: The Atlantic white-sided dolphin is a medium-sized marine mammal with a robust, streamlined body built for life in the cool waters of the North Atlantic. These energetic dolphins typically measure 6-9 feet long and weigh between 400-500 pounds, making them smaller than bottlenose dolphins but larger than harbor porpoises. Their most distinctive feature is their striking color pattern: a dark back, lighter sides with prominent white patches, and a pale belly. They have a short, thick beak and a tall, curved dorsal fin that cuts through the water as they surface to breathe.

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive white and yellowish patches along the sides that create bold racing stripes from head to tail, contrasting sharply with the dark gray to black back and pale belly

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized dolphin with a stocky, robust build and a relatively short, thick beak compared to bottlenose dolphins, appearing more compact and muscular in the water

idTips.label: Dorsal Fin
idTips.description: Tall, prominently curved dorsal fin that's dark colored and easily visible when the dolphin surfaces, often the first part you'll spot breaking the water

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Highly acrobatic and social, often seen leaping completely out of the water, bow-riding boats, and traveling in energetic pods of 10-50 individuals that create visible splashes and spray

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in deeper offshore waters rather than close to shore, typically in areas where the continental shelf drops off and water temperatures are cool

habitat: Atlantic white-sided dolphins prefer the deeper, cooler waters off New England's coast, typically found beyond the continental shelf in waters over 600 feet deep. They're most commonly spotted during whale watching trips that venture 20+ miles offshore, especially in areas where cold Labrador Current waters mix with warmer Gulf Stream waters. These dolphins favor the productive waters around Stellwagen Bank, Jeffrey's Ledge, and other underwater features where upwelling brings nutrients to the surface.

seasonality.spring: Dolphins begin moving closer to New England waters as temperatures warm, with sightings increasing in April and May. This is prime whale watching season when tour boats are most likely to encounter active pods.
seasonality.summer: Peak viewing season with the highest number of sightings from June through August. Dolphins are most active and acrobatic during warm summer months, often seen feeding alongside whales and seabirds.
seasonality.fall: Still commonly seen through September and October as they follow fish migrations. Water clarity is often excellent for viewing during calm fall days.
seasonality.winter: Sightings drop dramatically as dolphins move to warmer southern waters or stay in deeper offshore areas. Only occasionally spotted during winter whale watching trips.

funFact: Atlantic white-sided dolphins are incredible acrobats that can leap up to 20 feet out of the water — that's higher than most two-story houses! They seem to jump purely for joy, often performing synchronized leaps with their pod mates in what looks like an oceanic ballet performance.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with white-beaked dolphins, but Atlantic white-sided dolphins have yellowish side patches (not just white) and a darker overall coloration. Remember: 'white-sided' has the racing stripe pattern along the whole side, while 'white-beaked' dolphins have prominent white mainly on the beak and a more uniformly colored body.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'white-sided,' these dolphins actually have yellowish or tan patches mixed with white along their sides — the white designation comes from early descriptions when observers saw them from a distance. The scientific name Leucopleurus literally means 'white-sided' in Greek, cementing this somewhat imprecise but traditional name.
compareHints: Atlantic white-sided dolphins are the only species in their genus (Leucopleurus) found in New England waters, making them unique among local dolphins. Compared to the more familiar bottlenose dolphins in the same family, white-sided dolphins are more robust and stocky with shorter beaks, more contrasting color patterns, and much more acrobatic behavior. They're also more likely to be seen in large, energetic groups rather than the smaller pods typical of bottlenose dolphins.
